summary: Specifies AES-CMAC, an authentication algorithm that uses the CMAC mode from NIST with 128-bit AES. The document makes it conveniently available to the Internet community. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: AES-CMAC lets two parties with the same secret key check whether a message has changed and whether it came from someone who knows that key. The RFC explains how to calculate and verify the check value.

subtitle: A message authentication code built from AES and a shared secret key.

tldr.problem: A checksum can detect accidental changes, but it cannot establish that a message came from someone holding a secret key. AES-CMAC provides an authentication check based on AES.
tldr.mechanism: AES-CMAC chains AES encryption across message blocks. It derives two subkeys and uses one of them to prepare the final block, depending on whether that block is complete.
tldr.outcome: The RFC specifies AES-CMAC using AES-128 and includes test vectors. It is an Informational RFC, not an Internet Standards Track specification.

today: RFC 4493 is an Informational RFC and does not specify an Internet standard. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Purpose of AES-CMAC
sections.content:
RFC 4493 specifies an authentication algorithm called AES-CMAC. It uses the CMAC mode with AES-128 and makes the algorithm available to the Internet community.

A checksum or error-detecting code can detect accidental changes. A message authentication code (MAC) uses a secret key and is designed to detect unauthorized changes as well. The RFC describes AES-CMAC as having a security goal similar to HMAC and notes it can suit systems where AES is more readily available than a hash function.
sections.plainLanguage: A checksum can show that data changed by accident. AES-CMAC also uses a secret key to help detect changes made by someone without that key.

sections.title: Processing the Message Blocks
sections.content:
AES-CMAC takes a secret key, a message of any length, and the message length in octets. It divides the message into 128-bit blocks and processes them as a CBC-MAC chain: each block is combined with the previous result before AES encrypts it.

The final block has two cases. If the message has a positive length that is a multiple of the block size, the algorithm XORs the block with subkey K1. Otherwise, it adds a 1 bit followed by zero bits to complete the block and XORs it with K2. An empty message uses the incomplete-block case.

The default MAC is 128 bits. Truncation is allowed, but its length must be fixed before communication and remain unchanged for the lifetime of the key. The RFC says at least 64 bits should be used.
sections.plainLanguage: AES-CMAC processes each message block using the previous block's result. It prepares a complete final block differently from a short or empty final block.

sections.title: Deriving the Two Subkeys
sections.content:
The algorithm derives two 128-bit subkeys, K1 and K2, from the AES key. It first encrypts an all-zero 128-bit block with the key to obtain L.

To derive K1, it shifts L left by one bit. If the most significant bit of L was 1, it XORs the shifted value with the constant const_Rb. It derives K2 by applying the same shift-and-conditional-XOR operation to K1. The two subkeys are then used in message generation and verification.
sections.plainLanguage: The algorithm derives two subkeys from the main AES key. It uses one for a complete final block and the other when it must pad the final block.

sections.title: Generating and Verifying a MAC
sections.content:
To generate a MAC, the sender derives the subkeys, prepares the final block, and runs the AES chain from an all-zero starting value. The final AES output is the MAC. If the system uses a shortened MAC, it keeps the most significant bits.

To verify a received MAC, the recipient runs the same generation process on the message using the shared key and compares the result with the received value. The RFC defines the result as VALID when they match and INVALID when they do not. A valid result provides assurance of authenticity and integrity, but the RFC notes that this assurance is not absolute.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver calculates a fresh MAC from the message and shared key. A match supports the message's integrity and authenticity; a mismatch means the message is not authentic.

sections.title: Key Security and Test Vectors
sections.content:
AES-CMAC depends on AES, a secret key, and correct implementations at the participating systems. If the key is compromised or shared inappropriately, the algorithm does not provide authentication or integrity. The RFC says the key should be generated to meet the randomness requirements in RFC 4086 and kept safe.

The RFC includes test vectors for subkey generation and MACs over empty messages and messages of several lengths. These values allow implementations to compare their results with the document's examples.
sections.plainLanguage: AES-CMAC cannot protect a message if someone else obtains the shared key. The included test values help developers check that their calculation follows the specification.
